slides: Let's continue with relative speed, and look at chases.

slides.say: In a chase, both of them move the same way, and one tries to catch the other.
Now a new example. A runner runs at six kilometers per hour.
A cyclist rides behind her on the same road, at nine kilometers per hour.
At the start, the runner is nine kilometers ahead of him.
After one hour, the cyclist rode nine kilometers.
But the runner didn't wait. She ran six kilometers further.
So he gained only nine minus six, three kilometers. The gap is nine minus three, six.
at: The gap is nine minus three

slides.say: After two hours, he rode eighteen kilometers, and she ran twelve.
He gained three kilometers again. Six minus three is three.
After three hours, he rode twenty-seven kilometers, and she ran eighteen.
He gained three once more. Three minus three is zero. He catches her.
Look at the gap column. Nine, six, three, zero.

slides: Every hour, the gap closes by the same three kilometers.

slides.say: Why three? Because he rides nine, but she runs away six. Nine minus six is three.
Imagine the slow one stands still. Then the cyclist comes closer at only three kilometers per hour.

slides: So in a chase, we subtract the speeds.

slides.say: Now look at the moment he catches her, after three hours.
The runner ran eighteen kilometers, from her start to the meeting point.
The cyclist rode twenty-seven kilometers. He rode her nine-kilometer head start, and then her eighteen kilometers too.
So his distance minus her distance is the head start. Twenty-seven minus eighteen is nine.
He catches her when he has gained the whole starting gap.
He gains three kilometers every hour, and he needs nine. Nine divided by three is three hours.
So in a chase, the time is the starting gap divided by the difference of the speeds.
at: the time is the starting gap

slides.say: Now a new example. A bus drives at fifty kilometers per hour. A car drives behind it, at seventy.
At the start, the bus is ten kilometers ahead of the car.
It's a chase, so we subtract. The car gains seventy minus fifty, twenty kilometers every hour.
It needs to gain ten kilometers. Ten divided by twenty is half an hour.
So the car catches the bus after thirty minutes.
And what if the faster one is in front? Then the gap doesn't close. It grows.
Say the car is in front and drives away from the bus. The gap grows by seventy minus fifty, twenty kilometers every hour.
at: The gap grows by seventy minus fifty

slides.say: The same direction, so we still subtract the speeds.
Here's the classic mistake, and it's almost always in a chase.
The only distance that matters is the gap between them when the chase starts. Not the whole way they ride, and not where they end up.
Imagine the runner at a hundred kilometers per hour, and the cyclist at a hundred and two. They travel very far, but the gap still closes by only two kilometers every hour.
at: the gap still closes by only two

slides: So in a chase, we only look at the starting gap, and at the difference between the speeds.

slides.say: And when one of them leaves earlier, we first find the head start. That head start is the gap.
Now a new example. Dan walks from home at four kilometers per hour. Half an hour later, his sister rides after him at twelve kilometers per hour. When does she catch him?

slides: We solve it in two stages. In the first stage, only Dan walks. In the second stage, both of them move.

slides.say: So first, the head start. In half an hour, Dan walks four times a half, two kilometers.
at: Dan walks four times a half

slides.say: Now the second stage. His sister starts, so we mark her start time on the sketch. The gap between them is two kilometers.
at: The gap between them is two kilometers

slides.say: It's a chase, so we subtract. She gains twelve minus four, eight kilometers every hour.
Two divided by eight is a quarter of an hour. So she catches him fifteen minutes after she starts.
Now careful with the time in a chase. Is it counted from the chaser's start, or from the first one's start? We read the question, and we mark both start times on the sketch.
at: Is it counted from the chaser

slides.say: Now a new example. Ava starts running. Ben waits ten seconds, and then chases her on the same route. He catches her thirty seconds after Ava started. How many times as fast as Ava is Ben?
The thirty seconds are counted from Ava's start. So Ava runs thirty seconds, and Ben runs only thirty minus ten, twenty seconds.
at: Ben runs only thirty minus ten

slides.say: They both run the same distance, from the start to the meeting point. The distance is fixed, so the times flip, like in speed ratios.
at: The distance is fixed, so the times flip

slides.say: Ava's time to Ben's time is thirty to twenty, three to two. So Ben's speed is three halves of Ava's. He is one and a half times as fast.
at: thirty to twenty, three to two
one and a half times as fast

slides.say: Now change just the last part of the question. Ben still starts ten seconds after Ava. But suppose Ben catches Ava thirty seconds after Ben starts. Ben runs thirty seconds, and Ava runs ten more, forty.
Then Ben is forty over thirty, four thirds times as fast.
Two readings, two different answers. So always ask, from whose start is the time counted?
So let's sum it up. Toward each other, or apart, we add the speeds.
In a chase, we subtract them.
at: In a chase, we subtract them

slides.say: They meet when together they cover the whole gap. And the time is the gap divided by the relative speed.
at: the time is the gap divided

slides.say: Only the starting gap counts. And if one leaves earlier, we find the head start first.
And we mark every start time on the sketch, and ask from whose start the time is counted.

slides: Chases are where students slip, so take a moment to memorize this. I'll see you in the next video.
